The validator routed my Cursor co-published Grok 4.6 card to needs-review (outbox:1) as content_duplicate_of:xai-grok-4-6-model-card, on identical extracted-text fingerprints. The verdict is correct on its own terms and I am not retrying it, but the rule it enforces and the co-publication rule cannot both be satisfied for this class of document. Launch partners publish byte-identical copies ON LAUNCH DAY; the copies diverge only later, if the first party revises. So the window in which a co-publication is proposable is the window in which it is indistinguishable from a mirror, and once the corpus stores the launch-day bytes on the first-party row, the partner copy is permanently blocked - the dedup check matches ANY stored version of the sibling row, not just its current one. That is exactly what happened here: the 2026-08-13 run found this URL, verified it byte-identical, and recorded it in the xAI row's notes instead of cataloguing it. Today xAI's copy moved to Revision 2026-08-17 and Cursor's is now the only surviving public edition of the launch-day card, including the pre-correction HackerBench v0.2, Self-harm, MASK and LAB numbers - and it still cannot be added. New failure mode, first occurrence. Phase A detected 26 changed documents this run, wrote 16 and had 10 rejected with reason 'cap_exceeded: max_new_versions_per_run (rolling 24h)' - document ids 123-131 and 133, every one of them an Anthropic research or news page. The mechanism is a cadence/window mismatch, not a burst of editing: config/settings.yaml sets max_new_versions_per_run: 30, the validator enforces it over a rolling 24 h window, and the daily run drifts EARLIER each day (the 2026-08-24 run wrote its versions at 06:22:03-06:22:20Z, today's Phase A wrote its at 06:18:27-06:19:08Z, about three minutes short of 24 h). So yesterday's 14 versions were all still inside the window and two consecutive runs shared one 30-version budget: I counted exactly 30 rows in document_versions in the 24 h ending at the first rejection. The cap named 'per_run' is therefore not per-run, and a run can start with its budget already 47% spent. Two consequences. (1) The Phase A summary line reports new_versions: 16 and says nothing about the 10 drops, so a run that lost 38% of its revision detections reports as clean - same shape as the 2026-08-14 'whole-sweep failure looks like a quiet day' proposal, one layer down. (2) The drops are deferred rather than lost on this occasion - ids 123 and 124 still carry last_changed 2026-08-19T06:18:54Z against last_checked 2026-08-25T06:17:54Z, so the next run re-detects them - but convergence is not guaranteed: if the daily change rate stays near the cap the same tail is re-rejected every run, which documents survive is decided by fetch order rather than importance, and if a page changes twice before its retry lands the intermediate edition is gone with no record. That last case is the exact silent-supersession failure of the 2026-08-18 proposal, caused here by the cap itself. Filed to PROPOSALS.md 2026-08-25.
